'''''Agave lechuguilla''''' (common name in Chihuahua: ''lechuguilla'', meaning "small lettuce") is an ''[[Agave]]'' species [[endemism|found only]] in the [[Chihuahuan Desert]]. The plant flowers once in its life and then dies.

== Description ==
The plant reproduces most often through underground offshoots, creating large colonies.<ref name=":0" /> It also can flower at any time after the plant has reached three to 21 years of age, producing a leafless stalk that can reach {{convert|12|ft|m|abbr=off|order=flip}} in height.<ref name=":0" /> The flower clusters are located at the top and are funnel-shaped in purples, reds, and yellows.<ref name=":0" /> The plant dies after flowering in May–July.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Spellenberg |first=Richard |url=https://archive.org/details/nationalaudubons00spel/page/325/ |title=National Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers: Western Region |publisher=Knopf |year=2001 |isbn=978-0-375-40233-3 |edition=rev |page=325 |orig-date=1979}}</ref> The [[leaves]] are long, tough, and rigid, with very sharp, hard points that can easily penetrate clothing and even leather, giving the colloquial name "shin-daggers".

== Taxonomy ==
[[Charles Wright (botanist)|Charles Wright]] first collected the plant in 1849 and it was described by [[John Torrey]] in 1859.<ref name=":0" />

== Distribution and habitat ==
It is an [[indicator species]] in the [[Chihuahuan Desert]], the only place it is found.<ref>{{cite book |last=West |first=Steve |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=6gvFgUiFeGsC |title=Northern Chihuahuan Desert Wildflowers |publisher=Globe Pequot |year=2000 |isbn=978-1-56044-980-5 |page=44}}</ref> It typically grows on [[calcareous]] soils.<ref>{{cite book |last=Turner |first=Matt |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pIXpf4RRA1IC |title=Remarkable Plants of Texas: Uncommon Accounts of Our Common Natives |publisher=University of Texas Press |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-292-71851-7 |location=Austin |pages=109–113}}</ref>

== Ecology ==
The plant makes up a large part of the diet of the [[collared peccary]] (javelina) in some areas.<ref name="corn">Corn, J. L. and R. J. Warren. (1985). [https://www.jstor.org/pss/1380973 Seasonal food habits of the collared peccary in South Texas.] ''Journal of Mammalogy''. 66:1 155-59.</ref> Additionally, the flowers are a source of nutrients for insects, bats, and some birds. The plant is toxic to [[cattle]] and [[sheep]], however.<ref name="tox">[http://essmextension.tamu.edu/plants/toxics/detail.aspx?plantID=87 Lechuguilla.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120403104015/http://essmextension.tamu.edu/plants/toxics/detail.aspx?plantID=87|date=April 3, 2012}} Toxic plants of Texas. Texas A&M.</ref>

== Uses ==
The water stored in the flowering stalks of this plant, rich in salts and minerals, is sold in Mexico as a [[sport drink]]. Native Mexicans have used fibers from the leaves (commonly called ''[[istle|ixtle]]'').<ref name=":1" /> Roots of the plants were used as soap by [[Native Americans in the United States|Native Americans]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|title=Little Big Bend: Common, Uncommon, and Rare Plants of Big Bend National Park|last=Morey|first=Roy|date=2008|publisher=Texas Tech University Press|isbn=978-0-89672-613-0|location=Lubbock|pages=37|oclc=80359503}}</ref>
